description: We are a passionate team interested in Software Engineering, AI, Data Analysis, and Space Exploration. Our goal is to develop smart health monitoring software that tracks astronauts' health, visualizes real-time biometric data, detects unusual patterns, and provides early health alerts. We welcome developers, AI/ML enthusiasts, UI/UX designers, researchers, writers, and space lovers who want to contribute their skills and ideas to make future space missions safer!
summary:
We created our project based on "Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions" topic. 
We developed the Crew Vitals Console for observing astronaut health while on space missions, whether they’re for shorter periods or extended durations. In real-time, it monitors an astronaut’s vital signs such as heart rate, blood pressure, and oxygen levels. It also tracks body temperature, breathing rate, and heart rate variability.

In addition to physical parameters, there are other hazards in space missions related to radiation exposure and immune system changes that require monitoring. Also, there is always the concern about long-term effects on bone mass and other physiological systems due to weightlessness and microgravity conditions. Sleep issues can affect mental health, which must be monitored carefully throughout any space flight journey.

The console provides dashboards showing updates live with graphs representing trends over time. When necessary, alerts will be triggered automatically by our system. Personalized assessments help understand individual requirements better through our AI assistant providing guidance where needed alongside environment monitoring capabilities and activity tracking features included within the package itself offering emergency support whenever required without delay.
details:
Crew Vitals Console

1. What does the project do, and how does it work?

Our project, Crew Vitals Console, is a web-based health monitoring system developed to help astronauts monitor and manage their health during space missions. It provides two main interfaces: a personal health dashboard for astronauts and a crew monitoring console for mission commanders and flight surgeons.

The system collects and displays important health indicators, including heart rate, blood pressure, heart rate variability (HRV), oxygen levels, respiratory rate, and body temperature. It also monitors environmental conditions such as cabin pressure, oxygen, carbon dioxide, and space radiation.

The software evaluates health indicators using individual health baselines, risk assessment algorithms, and automated alert mechanisms. When unusual health conditions are detected, it generates alerts and recommends appropriate countermeasures.

The system also includes an AI-powered Aerospace Health Assistant that helps astronauts understand health information and provides health-related guidance. Additional features include:

• Personal Health Dashboard: Displays individual health measurements and health status.

• Crew Monitoring Console: Allows mission commanders to monitor crew health conditions.

• Space Weather Monitoring: Displays solar flares, solar energetic particle events, and geomagnetic storms using NASA's DONKI data.

• Live ISS Monitoring: Displays available real-time International Space Station cabin measurements.

• ISS Location Tracker: Shows the station's current position, altitude, speed, and orbital path.

• Immune System Monitoring: Estimates potential immune system risks associated with spaceflight.

• Long-Term Health Assessment: Models potential bone loss, muscle changes, sleep problems, and other long-duration mission risks.

• Reaction Time Test: Evaluates astronaut alertness and cognitive performance.

• Automated Health Alerts: Identifies unusual measurements and suggests appropriate actions.

• Daily Activity Tracking: Encourages astronauts to complete important health-related daily activities.

2. What benefits does the project have?

The project provides several important benefits:

• Helps astronauts monitor their health continuously throughout a mission.

• Identifies unusual health measurements and potential health risks at an early stage.

• Supports independent health monitoring when communication with Earth is delayed or unavailable.

• Provides mission commanders with an overview of crew health conditions.

• Helps astronauts understand their health status through visual dashboards, graphs, and an AI assistant.

• Supports long-term health management by tracking potential effects of microgravity, radiation, isolation, and other spaceflight conditions.

• Provides space environment information that helps astronauts understand environmental risks.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

Our main goal is to improve astronaut safety and support successful space missions by providing an accessible and intelligent health monitoring solution.

We aim to reduce the risks associated with long-duration space missions by helping astronauts identify health changes, take appropriate actions, and manage their health more independently.

The project could also contribute to the future development of autonomous astronaut healthcare systems, particularly for missions to Mars and other destinations where immediate communication with Earth may not be possible.

4. What tools, programming languages, and software did we use?

We developed the project using the following technologies:

• JavaScript: Main programming language used to implement the application's functionality and logic.

• React.js: Used to develop the interactive user interface and reusable components.

• HTML5: Used to structure the web application.

• CSS3: Used to design the interface, dashboards, charts, and responsive layouts.

• Vite: Used as the development server and build tool.

• Recharts: Used to create interactive health monitoring graphs and visualizations.

• NASA APIs: Used to retrieve real space weather information from NASA DONKI.

• NASA ISS Live Data Feed: Used to retrieve available live ISS cabin measurements.

• Lightstreamer: Used to connect to the live ISS data feed.

• Local Storage: Used to save application settings and health-related mission data locally.

• Vitest: Used to perform automated software testing.

The application is primarily software-based and does not require additional physical monitoring hardware for its current demonstration. Health telemetry is simulated, while selected environmental and space-related information can be retrieved from live external sources.

5. How is our project creative and innovative?

Our project combines several health monitoring and space exploration features into one integrated platform rather than providing only a basic health dashboard.

One of its creative aspects is the use of personalized health baselines. Instead of relying only on general reference values, the system compares measurements against an astronaut's individual health patterns to identify unusual changes.

Another innovative feature is its autonomous monitoring approach. The system considers communication delays between Earth and spacecraft, particularly during Mars missions, and supports onboard health assessment and countermeasure workflows without requiring an immediate response from Earth.

We also integrated space weather monitoring, live ISS environmental information, an ISS tracking map, immune risk assessment, cognitive reaction testing, and an AI-powered health assistant into the same application.

Additionally, the interface includes interactive visualizations and daily health activities to make health monitoring more understandable and engaging for astronauts.

6. What factors did our team consider?

During development, our team considered several important factors:

1. Astronaut Safety: Health monitoring and early identification of potential health risks were our highest priorities.

2. Spaceflight Conditions: We considered microgravity, radiation exposure, isolation, confinement, and the challenges of living in a closed spacecraft environment.

3. Communication Delays: We considered the possibility of delayed or unavailable communication with Earth during deep-space missions.

4. Long-Term Health Effects: We considered potential changes in cardiovascular health, immune function, bone density, sleep, and cognitive performance.

5. Data Reliability: We distinguished simulated astronaut health measurements from genuine live environmental data and NASA-related research information.

6. User Experience: We designed the interface to be understandable and accessible to astronauts and mission personnel.

7. Offline and Autonomous Operation: We considered the importance of providing useful onboard monitoring and decision-support capabilities.

8. Scalability: We designed the application around different mission environments, including spacecraft, space stations, lunar surfaces, and Mars missions.

9. Scientific References: We considered NASA research and relevant standards when developing health risk models and environmental monitoring features.

Overall, our project aims to provide a comprehensive, intelligent, and user-friendly health monitoring platform that supports astronaut well-being, independent decision-making, and safer future space exploration.
